subject: SecureHealth: connectivity recommendation — peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S VPN

Subject: Redwood Private deployment — connectivity options (quick ask)

Hi Mina,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday — team was impressed with the latency numbers. Our security and networking teams asked for a short write-up comparing three connectivity patterns for a Private deployment: VPC peering (cross-account), AWS PrivateLink (interface VPC endpoints), and site-to-site VPN into our VPC. Main constraints:
- No internet-exposed endpoints; all traffic must be private (AWS internal).
- Support multi-AZ, potential multi-region later (primary us-east-1 today).
- Minimal networking changes on our side (we manage the customer VPC).
- Auditability (flow logs, connection-level logs) and key rotation / KMS compatibility.

Could you send a recommendation and call out tradeoffs (security posture, operational complexity, perf/cost, transitive routing)? I attached our high-level requirements.

Appreciate it —
Alice
Network Architect, SecureHealth

Alice — thanks for the prompt and the attachment. Looping in Lauren (solutions lead) and Marcus (infra architect) to make sure we cover operational controls and the runtime implications.

High-level recommendation up-front: use PrivateLink (interface endpoints) for control-plane-like traffic (API/control plane, metrics) and VPC Peering for high-throughput, low-latency data paths if you want direct L3 reachability. Site-to-site VPN is a fallback for quick proofs-of-concept or if your org requires IP-level isolation and you don't want cross-account peering.

I'll attach a short diagram and a one-page tradeoff table, and then propose a few follow-ups:
- Quick architecture sketch for each option (we can share a template you can hand to your NetEng)
- Cost ballpark (egress and endpoint charges)
- Audit/logging implications + how Redwood Surface (Private) surfaces connection metadata in Console & audit logs

We'll aim to get this to you by EOD Wednesday PST.

— Mina
Account Exec, Redwood Inference

Hi Alice — Marcus from Infra. Quick technical notes to unpack Mina's summary below, with pros/cons from a runtime/ops perspective: 

VPC Peering (cross-account):
- Pros: L3 connectivity, no additional per-flow endpoint charges, low latency for intra-region traffic. Good if you need the Redwood private nodes to be addressable directly from your hosts.
- Cons: No transitive routing (can't automatically traverse from your VPC to other connected VPCs). If SecureHealth wants to connect many VPCs to Redwood, peering can become operationally heavy. Also requires careful route table management and CIDR planning to avoid overlap.

AWS PrivateLink (Interface endpoints):
- Pros: Restricts traffic to the service endpoint; provides stronger isolation (Redwood presents an endpoint service and you create ENIs in your VPC). Easier to expose specific ports/paths rather than whole subnets. Works well with cross-account access and doesn't require CIDR coordination.
- Cons: Per-GB and per-hour charges for the interface endpoints and data processing costs — depends on throughput. Slightly higher latency than peering but predictable and secure. Not ideal if you need arbitrary L3 peer connectivity (it's service-level).

Site-to-site VPN (IPSec):
- Pros: Fast to stand up for POC or if company policy requires S2S. Allows full L3 reachability and can be encrypted with customer-managed keys.
- Cons: Lower throughput; latency variability; management of tunnels and BGP sessions; less suitable as a long-term production path for heavy LLM inference traffic unless you use dedicated hardware or AWS VPN CloudHub/Transit Gateway options.

Operational notes:
- For production we recommend a hybrid pattern: PrivateLink for control-plane and telemetry (logs/metrics/health checks) + VPC Peering for the high-throughput inference data plane if SecureHealth controls a single customer VPC per region. If SecureHealth plans multiple VPCs across teams/regions, evaluate Transit Gateway with VPC attachments (cost vs simplicity tradeoff) or use PrivateLink across accounts with shared services.
- Auditability: All options support VPC Flow Logs; PrivateLink and peering can be observed from ENI-level logs. Redwood will emit request-level audit events to the Private control plane and to your SIEM (we can provide a CloudWatch/CloudTrail ingestion guide).
- KMS/HSM: No changes required for PrivateLink or peering; data at rest and keys remain in your account if you bring your own key for storage or for TLS termination where applicable.

I'll drop a short cost model for these patterns into the doc.

— Marcus
Infra Architect, Redwood Inference

Alice, 

Adding operational controls and rollout guidance from product/solutions perspective: 
- Canary/rollout: If you choose peering for data plane, we suggest a canary host group (two subnets) in your VPC that receives traffic first. Redwood supports routing rules by source subnet, so you can incrementally shift production traffic.
- Fallbacks: Configure PrivateLink as a fallback path for control-plane calls and for failover when peering connectivity is disrupted.
- SLAs & HA: For peering, ensure cross-AZ subnets and redundant ENIs on our side. For PrivateLink, ensure multiple AZ endpoint configuration and health-check integration.
- Documentation we will share: BGP config snippets (if you go S2S+BGP), Route table examples for peering, endpoint service creation steps for PrivateLink.

Next steps: propose a 45-minute workshop (NetEng + Redwood Infra/Product) to finalize the pattern and produce a handoff doc that your NetEng can implement. Available windows: Tue 3/2 (PST) or Thu 3/4 (PST).

— Lauren Bishop
